# The Country of Night

In Mammoth Cave in Kentucky, park rangers perform a small ceremony. They lead visitors deep underground, past the last gray seep of daylight, into a chamber where no natural light has ever reached, and then—after a warning—they switch off the electric lamps. What follows is not dimness. Dimness implies a remainder, some faint residue to squint against. This is absence, total and immediate. Your hand vanishes before your eyes. You cannot see the person beside you, cannot see your own feet, cannot confirm that you have eyes at all. There is usually a ripple of nervous laughter, then silence. After a minute or two, people begin reporting shapes—rings of pale light, drifting forms—that exist nowhere except in their own visual cortices, firing hopefully into the void. The brain, denied input, starts inventing it. Then the ranger says something that lands differently on everyone who hears it: *This is what night used to be.*

Most of us will never meet darkness like that. We live downstream of a great conquest, one so complete we've forgotten there was ever a war. Within a few generations—less time than a single long human life spans—night was defeated, paved over, converted into a slightly darker version of afternoon. And yet I want to argue that something enormous was quietly lost in the victory, because night was not merely an inconvenience to be engineered away. It was a country, with its own laws, its own customs, its own economies and pleasures and terrors. We didn't improve it. We evicted ourselves from it, and we have been sleeping badly in exile ever since.

Consider first how expensive darkness's opposite used to be. For nearly all of human history, light after sunset was a luxury item. Tallow candles—rendered animal fat, foul-smelling and guttering—were dear enough that a laborer thought twice before lighting one. Beeswax burned cleaner but cost more. Whale oil was for the wealthy. Peasants made do with rushlights: dried reeds dipped in grease, sputtering on an iron holder, giving off barely more illumination than a match. Firewood was fuel, not light. When the sun went down, most people went to bed not out of rustic virtue but out of simple arithmetic. The very word *curfew* descends from the Old French *cuevrefeu*—"cover fire"—a bell rung in medieval towns ordering hearths smothered for the night. Moonlight was infrastructure. A full moon meant you could walk to the next village, finish bringing in the harvest, see the face of the person you were talking to. The harvest moon earned its name honestly: it was a gift of free overtime.

And what did people do with all that enforced darkness? They slept—but not the way we do. The historian Roger Ekirch, combing through diaries, letters, court records, medical manuals, and prayer books going back centuries, documented something startling: before the modern era, Western sleep came in two acts. People went to bed a few hours after dusk, slept deeply for three or four hours—the "first sleep"—then woke naturally around midnight and stayed awake for an hour or two, a quiet interlude sometimes called "the watch." During the watch, people prayed, stoked the fire, talked with bedfellows, made love, smoked, brewed beer, or simply lay thinking while the house breathed around them. Then came the "second sleep," which carried them to dawn. References to this rhythm are everywhere once you know to look for them—Chaucer speaks of it, as do countless ordinary diarists—and it wasn't framed as insomnia. Waking in the middle of the night was as unremarkable as waking in the morning. In laboratory studies decades later, the physiologist Thomas Wehr found that when modern volunteers were given fourteen hours of darkness each day, within weeks they spontaneously reverted to exactly this pattern: two sleeps, divided by a serene, meditative wakefulness. The segmented night, it turns out, may be the human default. We are the anomaly.

That midnight interval was only part of night's culture. Evening, in the age of expensive light, belonged to stories. With work done and firelight gathered around, someone would talk—epics, ghost tales, genealogies, jokes, scripture, gossip from the next valley. Many cultures formally reserved certain kinds of stories for darkness; telling them in daylight was bad luck or bad manners. Firelight plus a human voice was the original cinema, and it was interactive: the audience groaned, heckled, demanded the wolf part again. Night was also, unavoidably, social in a cramped physical way. Families shared rooms and often beds; warmth was pooled like money. Whole relationships were conducted in the dark's privacy, whispered across pillows, conducted in a register of honesty that daylight, with its witnesses, rarely permitted.

None of this is to romanticize it entirely—night was genuinely feared, and reasonably so. The word *nightmare* preserves an old belief: the *mare*, a demon that sat on sleepers' chests. Bandits worked the roads after sundown. City dwellers hired link boys—children carrying flaming torches—to walk them home through streets with no lighting at all. But fear and freedom braided together strangely in the dark. Night was the one jurisdiction daylight's authorities couldn't fully police. Under its cover, lovers met, dissidents printed pamphlets, servants gossiped, poets wandered, thieves thrived, and anyone at all could be briefly, gloriously unobserved. Night was the commons of the self.

And above it all hung the ceiling of stars—which is the part of the old night hardest for us to even imagine. To a farmer in 1700, the Milky Way was not a special occasion. It was a fact of existence, a luminous river splitting the sky, impossible to miss on any clear moonless night. The stars were simultaneously clock, calendar, compass, and scripture. Sailors steered by them; Polynesian navigators crossed thousands of miles of open Pacific holding star paths in memory. Farmers watched the Pleiades to time their planting. The Magi followed a star to a manger; Aboriginal Australians read entire moral histories into constellations of darkness between the stars. As late as 1889, Vincent van Gogh, looking out the window of an asylum in Saint-Rémy-de-Provence—a modest town, already partly electrifying—still saw a sky alive enough to paint swirling, blazing, unforgettable. He was painting a normal Tuesday night.

Then came the conquest. London's Pall Mall was lit by gas in 1807, and the century that followed turned streetlighting into a civic arms race. Paris glowed; the "City of Light" earned its nickname partly from its boulevards burning bright as day. This was celebrated, rightly, as progress: fewer accidents, less crime, commerce extended into the evening. In 1879 Edison patented a practical incandescent bulb, and the grid began its spread—first downtowns, then whole cities, then everything. In 1935 the Cincinnati Reds played the first night baseball game under newly installed floodlights, and a sport that had belonged to afternoons became an entertainment of evenings. Radio arrived, then television, then the screen in every pocket, each one a private sun. Today, satellites photograph the Earth at night and produce images that look like a neural network: continents webbed with light, coastlines traced in gold. Night has become a scheduling problem, then an aesthetic choice, then, effectively, obsolete. The country of night has been annexed, parcel by parcel, into the empire of day.

The costs arrived slowly enough that we never sent an invoice. Start with the sky. A landmark 2016 study calculated that more than eighty percent of humanity now lives under light-polluted skies, and that the Milky Way is hidden from more than a third of the world's people—including sixty percent of Europeans and nearly eighty percent of North Americans. For them, the galaxy exists only as photographs. Children grow up assuming "stars" means a scattering of a dozen faint dots, when a truly dark sky holds thousands, resolving into that vast spiral arm we live inside. We have done something no generation before us could have conceived: we have made the universe invisible to ourselves.

The costs to the body are subtler but better measured. Human physiology is built around darkness; the hormone melatonin, which governs sleep timing and does repair work throughout the body, is produced only in the dark, and its production is suppressed by light—especially the blue-heavy wavelengths our screens emit with such enthusiasm. The World Health Organization's cancer agency classifies shift work that disrupts circadian rhythms as a probable human carcinogen. Hundreds of millions of people now sleep less and worse than their bodies require, staring at ceilings at 2 a.m., and we treat this as a personal failing rather than the predictable result of having abolished the night while keeping its hours.

Other species never agreed to the annexation. On beaches worldwide, sea turtle hatchlings instinctively crawl toward the brighter horizon—which, for a hundred million years, meant the star-and-moon-glinted ocean. Now it often means a beachfront hotel, and they march inland to die on highways. By some estimates, hundreds of millions of birds collide with illuminated buildings in North America each year, drawn off course by skies they mistake for navigable. Moths, which evolved to steer by the distant moon, spiral fatally into porch lights; entire insect populations decline around chronic illumination, taking pollination down with them. Ecosystems run on schedules written in darkness, and we have rewritten the clocks without asking.

Perhaps the least measurable loss is interior. The midnight watch—that drowsy, unhurried hour—is precisely the mental state in which the mind does its strangest, best work: reverie, half-dream, the slow association that solves problems daylight logic can't touch. History's legends agree on this; stories tell of chemists and mathematicians who woke from sleep holding answers their waking minds had chased for months. We have replaced that hour with feeds and notifications, infinite content engineered to fill every unfenced moment, and we wonder why our thoughts feel shallow. Boredom was the incubator. We fumigated it.

And yet the case for reclaiming darkness isn't only about repairing losses. It's about what the dark uniquely gives. Stand under a genuinely black sky—far from any city, on a moonless night—and wait. Psychologists studying awe find that it reliably shrinks the ego: people who regularly encounter vast things become measurably more generous, more humble, less rumination-bound. The night sky is the original overwhelming vastness, available free of charge. Pascal wrote that "the eternal silence of these infinite spaces frightens me"—but there is another reading, equally true. The iron in your blood and the calcium in your bones were forged inside dying stars; looking up is looking at your own raw materials, scattered and burning. The dark sky doesn't diminish you. It files you correctly.

Darkness also restores the two things modern life claims to want most: rest and mystery. Real sleep wants real dark—not the amber glow of the streetlamp through curtains, not the standby LED winking from the television. And mystery, whatever our optimization culture believes, is not a defect to be eliminated. Not everything benefits from illumination. Imagination lives at the edge of sight; children understand this perfectly, which is why the space under the bed is terrifying and the bottom of the garden enchanted. The Romantics knew it—Novalis wrote his *Hymns to the Night*, Chopin composed nocturnes, Whistler painted the Thames as veils of blue-black mist. Night was the muse of inwardness. It still is, wherever we permit it.

The good news is that the old country still issues visas. Around the world, designated dark-sky reserves protect patches of authentic night, and you don't need one to begin: any moonless evening, far from a city, will do. Bring a red-filtered flashlight if you must, then turn even that off. Wait thirty minutes—the full adaptation of your night vision takes about that long, which is why most people never experience it, checking their phones every ninety seconds and resetting the clock. Then look up. The stars return gradually, then suddenly: dozens, then hundreds, then the faint gray river of the galaxy itself, so large it stops registering as an object and becomes a place. You are inside it. You always were.

Back in Mammoth Cave, the ranger eventually switches the lights on, and there is a collective exhale—relief and, if you're paying attention, a small grief. The darkness lifts like water draining. But it leaves something behind: the knowledge that the dark was never empty. It was full—of stars, of sleep's second act, of stories, of the mind's own phosphorescence. Darkness was here first. Light is the guest, and lately the guest has eaten the house. So tonight, try this: turn off one lamp earlier than usual. Sit in the dark and let your eyes do their slow, ancient work. Somewhere overhead, behind the orange haze, the old country is still there—patient, unmapped, waiting for us to look up and remember the way home.
